column2: A survey published in two thousand seven tested two hundred seventy-seven internal medicine residents in Connecticut. Eighty-eight percent felt at least fairly confident about p-values.
Only about fifty-nine percent picked the answer marked correct. A later paper argued even that answer is wrong.
Your test comes back positive. It gives a false alarm to five percent of people without the disease.
So is there a ninety-five percent chance you have it?
Count people instead. Ten thousand of them, and one in a hundred has the disease.
That's one row of a hundred. Say the test catches ninety.
The other nine thousand nine hundred don't have it. Five percent of them still test positive. Four hundred ninety-five false alarms.
Now gather everyone who tested positive.
Ninety have the disease, and four hundred ninety-five don't. So only about fifteen percent of the positives have it.
Five percent was a share of people without the disease. Your question is a share of people who tested positive.
Take the same test to a clinic where one person in ten has the disease.
The test hasn't changed. It still catches nine in ten, and still gives five percent of the rest a false alarm.
So will a positive result mean more here, or less?
Count again. A thousand have the disease, and nine hundred of them test positive.
Of the other nine thousand, five percent is four hundred fifty false alarms.
Gather the positives. Nine hundred of the thirteen hundred fifty have the disease. That's two in three.
So here a positive result means about sixty-seven percent, not fifteen.
Why? The false alarms barely moved, but the test caught ten times as many people with the disease.
So keep the two apart. A false alarm rate is not the chance a positive result is right. And neither one is a p-value.
A p-value answers a question about a study instead. To find it, we first build an imaginary world where the treatment does nothing.
Here are the twenty pairs again, matched before treatment. In each pair, a fair coin chose who got the treatment.
Shorter recovery is better, so we decide in advance. A pair favours the treatment if its treated patient recovered first.
Now suppose the treatment changed nobody's recovery. Each patient would have recovered at the same time either way.
Here's what happened. In fifteen of the twenty pairs, the treated patient recovered first.
If the treatment did nothing, who recovered first stays fixed. Only the coins could have landed differently. Toss them again.
And again, and again. Each toss gives its own count.
The twenty coins can land in just over a million ways, all equally likely. Count them all.
Same patients, coins tossed again. This world assumes the treatment did nothing, so it can't say how likely that is.
In this world, how often do fifteen or more pairs favour the treatment?
